newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's NATO celebration bitter-sweet for Walesa.
newsitem.headline: Poland's NATO celebration bitter-sweet for Walesa.

text.p: Poland's invitation to NATO and U.S. President Bill Clinton's Warsaw visit on Thursday were a bitter-sweet success for Lech Walesa's long efforts to build a democratic Poland bound securely to the West.
Walesa's narrow election defeat in 1995 meant his ex-communist foe Aleksander Kwasniewski got the glory.
Walesa looked on from the stands while President Kwasniewski swapped eloquent speeches with Clinton before crowds of thousands in Warsaw's Castle Square.
After a brief meeting of his own with Clinton later on, Walesa was guarded and sounded less than overjoyed.
He said he thanked Clinton for his role in NATO's invitation at this week's Madrid summit for Poland to start entry talks but stressed that there was still far to go.

"I also pointed out that we have to finish this activity, this is just the start," Walesa said, recalling that in 1993 he had secured Russian President Boris Yeltsin's agreement to Polish NATO membership but this had been quickly reversed.
Walesa told public television he had told Clinton that full entry, planned for 1999, had to be quickly concluded.
Walesa led the Solidarity union's victory over communism in 1989, when Kwasniewski was in the communist government.
As Poland's first democratic president he was an early champion of its rapid NATO entry at a time when Kwasniewski's social democrats rejected the idea or thought it premature.
The ruling ex-communists have since fervently embraced it.

Kwasniewski, a fluent English speaker who is more eloquent and elegant than former shipyard worker Walesa, has won international praise for his efforts towards NATO membership, a goal supported by 80 percent of Poles of almost all political hues.
In his speech hailing the NATO invitation, Kwasniewski paid tribute to politicians since 1989, mostly his political foes, who had paved the way for this week's foreign policy success.
He started with Walesa, and the crowd interrupted with a long roar of applause while the white-moustached ex-president stood in a characteristic arms-raised victory poise.
Walesa's response to Kwasniewski's tribute and his rival's progress in advancing the NATO bid was typically brusque.
"I'm very pleased that not only did we defeat the communist system, we also forced those people to work on our principles and on a direction set by us," said Walesa, now in opposition.
